newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav state media target of opposition anger.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav state media target of opposition anger.

text.p: Like most broadcasters, the first news bulletin of 1997 on Yugoslavia's state television RTS showed huge celebrations from cities like New York, London and Sydney to usher in the new year.

But RTS ignored the one aspect of the Belgrade celebrations which made news for the international broadcasters -- a street party in central Belgrade attended by 250,000 revellers opposed to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
As on most days, state-controlled RTS news ignored the opposition's long-running protest against voting fraud that robbed it of victory in local elections on November 17.
"They (official media) live in cloud cuckoo land," said one opposition supporter who declined to be named. "RTS is our country's greatest purveyor of fiction."
Since the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties and their student allies launched daily protests 46 days ago, much of their anger has focused on RTS and the socialist daily Politika.
On New Year's Day, 10,000 students marched passed the RTS building blowing whistles and banging pots, pans and drums to drown out the evening newscast symbolically.
In an earlier gesture, protesters lit candles outside RTS and Politika to mourn "the death of truth".
Milosevic's stranglehold on the media has meant that people in the provinces have little idea of the chaos in the capital that is daily undermining 50 years of socialist rule.

On December 24, Milosevic brought thousands of people from rural towns and villages beyond the reach of Belgrade-based independent media, to join a counter-rally that resulted in running street battles between the two sides.

"What is going on?" asked a bewildered pensioner from the country who saw thousands of opposition supporters marching towards her. "I didn't know anyone was unhappy with our government. No one told us there might be trouble here."
The violence left one man dead and at least 50 people injured, including one man shot in the head by a supporter of the Socialist party (SPS).
Officially, half a million people joined the official "Rally for Serbia" in a spontaneous expression of support for the authorities.
Independent estimates put the made-for-television crowd at between 30,000 and 40,000.
In its reports, RTS made no mention of the violence or the 150,000 opposition supporters who marched through the city streets at the same time.

"My friend in Germany called the other day to find out how we are coping here," said a student named Jovan. "It seems he knows more about what is going on than my parents who live in a village barely 150 kilometres (93 miles) away."
"Those poor (pro-government) sods," said Milos Vasic of the independent weekly news magazine Vreme (Time). "They came here and got beaten up because they believed RTS."

"But the situation is now changing. They all would have gone back home and told their friends what realy happened here, and now I think people are starting to see through the lies. They are looking elsewhere for their news."
Vasic said since the start of the crisis, support has boomed for the few independent news outlets still allowed to operate.

Vreme's circulation has doubled to around 60,000, while independent radio B-92, whose signal covers only metropolitan Belgrade, has increased its regular audience from 300,000 to between 700,000 and one million.
"I think Milosevic's rule is unravelling," Vasic said.
"Even the journalists at RTS have had enough. Our sources tell us only four people with bodyguards write the daily news, and three of those listen to B-92 to hear what they can't report."
